title: Coral and the Harbor
premise: In 1748, in the fog-bound harbor town of Saltmere, apprentice clockmaker Freya Ashgrove is summoned to repair the observatory's failing master clock and keeps her head down among the powerful men who frequent it. When an abandoned child is left at the observatory door with a note ordering everyone to forget his face, Freya recognizes him as the missing son of a smuggler hanged on fabricated evidence — evidence forged by the very magistrate who now funds the observatory. As she restores the clock, she discovers its mechanism was deliberately altered to falsify the tide records that sealed the smuggler's trial, and she races to document the truth before the magistrate's allies rewrite the harbor's history. The book ends with Freya testifying at a reopened inquiry, the master clock striking honestly for the first time in years, and the boy — now under her guardianship — watching from the gallery as Saltmere chooses memory over convenience.
about_author: Quentin Ashgrove is the pen name of a former maritime museum archivist who spent a decade cataloguing eighteenth-century harbor ledgers and tide tables. Ashgrove writes historical fiction about ordinary tradespeople caught in the machinery of official history.

chapters.title: The Clock That Lies About Tides
chapters.summary: Freya arrives at the observatory to repair the master clock, immediately sensing something wrong in its escapement. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: cautious curiosity; she is an outsider among gentlemen and determined to stay invisible.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: During a storm, a mute boy is left at the observatory entrance with a note demanding his face be forgotten. The astronomer wants him gone by morning; Freya quietly takes him in. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: reluctant tenderness awakening her protective instincts.

chapters.title: What the Escapement Hides
chapters.summary: Repairing the clock, Freya finds a modified gear that skews the recorded tides — the same records used to convict smuggler Tomas Wren two years ago. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: dawning dread as craft becomes evidence.

chapters.title: The Widow Wren
chapters.summary: Freya seeks out Tomas Wren's widow, who confirms the boy is her son and begs Freya to let sleeping dogs lie for the child's safety. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: loyalty to the living pulling against duty to the dead.

chapters.title: Gentlemen of the Observatory Society
chapters.summary: At a society dinner, Magistrate Corliss praises the observatory's 'impeccable records' while probing Freya about her repairs. She realizes he knows what the clock once did. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Ledger
chapters.summary: Freya begins a secret ledger documenting the altered mechanism, enlisting a sympathetic printer's devil to copy tide tables from the burned customs house archives. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: quiet courage; justice built page by page outside the law.

chapters.title: Corliss Closes the Case
chapters.summary: Corliss declares the Wren matter settled forever and has the observatory sealed for 'renovation,' threatening anyone who disputes the record. The boy is nearly seized. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: the walls closing in; belonging itself becomes dangerous.

chapters.title: Ninety-Nine Hours
chapters.summary: Learning the inquiry into harbor charters convenes when the charter ship docks, Freya has four days to finish the ledger, restore the clock to truthful timekeeping, and find a witness willing to speak. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: desperate momentum against the calendar.

chapters.title: The Striking of the Hour
chapters.summary: Climax: before the assembled inquiry, Freya demonstrates the falsified escapement live, then releases the repaired clock so its corrected chimes contradict twenty years of doctored logs. The widow Wren testifies; Corliss unravels. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into triumph.

chapters.title: Coral and the Harbor
chapters.summary: Months later, the inquiry vindicates Wren posthumously, Corliss faces trial, and Freya gains formal standing as the observatory's clockmaker — and guardianship of the boy, who speaks his first word: her name. POV: Freya. Emotional beat: belonging earned, not granted; time set right.
